title: Deques
lead: An Essential section on the deque, a sequence that grows and shrinks at both ends, and on two ways to keep one in arrays; the DualArrayDeque is Advanced. Lists are indexed from 0. ODS’s “LIFO Queue” is the stack of Section 3.1. Its lemma on balance() uses Section 1.5’s potential method as a counter: each call that does not rebalance raises Φ by at most 1, so the calls before a costly balance() pay for it.
notes: The other paragraphs of ODS’s subsection on the Queue, Stack and Deque interfaces are left out here, the FIFO Queue being Section 3.2’s, and so are ODS’s exercises, which have no published answers.
exercise_notes: Exercism’s linked-list, held from Section 2.6, is a doubly linked deque: its tests are the canonical data’s, played by a small driver in the starter, less the case on deleting a value that is not there, which the Python track drops and answers with an error; its Python reference is the Python track’s example and its JavaScript reference the AI’s. Kattis’s Integer Lists has a sample only, so its other tests and both references are the AI’s, checked against a direct simulation. MIT 6.006’s Problem Session 1, problem 1-3, held from Section 2.2, is in exercises-nc.json, keyed by a link to MIT’s worked solution. ODS Exercises 2.6, 2.8 and 2.9, and Exercise 2.7 held from Section 2.2, have no tests of their own and are left out, as are SICP’s Exercise 3.23 (written, for Scheme), the unkeyed pythonds exercises and Kattis’s teque; ODS’s test_arraydeque.py and test_dualarraydeque.py, trekhleb’s deque tests and TheAlgorithms’ double_ended_queue.py are tests with no printed statement.

exercises.changes: Your LinkedList provides push, pop, shift, unshift, delete and len (count() in JavaScript); the tests are the canonical data’s operations, played by the run(ops) the starter gives, less the case on deleting a value that is not in the list. The specification’s note on linked lists in general is left out.
exercises.prompt:
You are working on a project to develop a train scheduling system for a busy railway network.

You've been asked to develop a prototype for the train routes in the scheduling system. Each route consists of a sequence of train stations that a given train stops at.

Your team has decided to use a doubly linked list to represent each train route in the schedule. Each station along the train's route will be represented by a node in the linked list.

You don't need to worry about arrival and departure times at the stations. Each station will simply be represented by a number.

Routes can be extended, adding stations to the beginning or end of a route. They can also be shortened by removing stations from the beginning or the end of a route.

Sometimes a station gets closed down, and in that case the station needs to be removed from the route, even if it is not at the beginning or end of the route.

The size of a route is measured not by how far the train travels, but by how many stations it stops at.

exercises.changes: Only the sample is the source’s; the other tests are written for this book from the statement, and a solution must take time linear in the input.
exercises.prompt:
The programming language Better And Portable Code (BAPC) is a language for working with lists of integers. The language has two built-in functions: ‘R’ (reverse) and ‘D’ (drop). The function ‘R’ reverses its input list, and ’D’ drops the first element of its input and returns the rest, or gives an error in case its input is an empty list. To get more advanced behavior, functions can be composed: “AB” is the function that first applies ‘A’ to its input and then ‘B’ to the resulting list. For example, “RDD” is a function that reverses a list and then drops the first two elements. Unfortunately, our BAPC interpreter has bit rotted, so we ask you to write a new one. Given a BAPC program and its input, return its output or “error” in case ‘D’ is applied to an empty list. Lists are represented as the character ‘[’ followed by a comma-separated list of integers followed by the character ‘]’. Notice that the input and output lists can be quite long. Input On the first line one positive number: the number of test cases, at most 100. After that per test case:
  • one line with a string $p$ $(1\le \text {length}(p) \le 100\,000)$: a BAPC program, consisting of the characters ‘R’ and ‘D’.
  • one line with an integer $n$ $(0\le n \le 100\,000)$: the number of elements in the input.
  • one line with a list of $n$ integers in the form $[x_1, \ldots ,x_ n]$ $(1\le x_ i \le 100)$: the input list.
Output Per test case:
  • one line with the resulting integer list or “error” in case of an error.

referents.label: j, the cell that holds list position 0
i, the list position a call names
front, the ArrayStack that holds the first part of the list, reversed
back, the ArrayStack that holds the rest of the list

footnotes.html: Here $a[0],\ldots,a[i-1]$ name the list’s first $i$ elements, not the array’s first cells: they sit at $a[j],\ldots,a[(j+i-1)\bmod \mathrm{length}(a)]$, where $\mathrm{get}(i)$ above finds them. The same holds for $a[i],\ldots,a[n-1]$ in this paragraph and for the ranges named in the paragraph on $\mathrm{remove}(i)$.
The second operation is $\mathrm{remove}(i)$, as the figure’s own caption says.

This holds where $n/2$ is the real quotient, as here and in the Python listing, whose $\mathtt{/}$ divides exactly. ODS’s Java and C++ listings divide $n$ by 2 in whole numbers, so when $n$ is odd and $i=(n-1)/2$ they shift $a[i],\ldots,a[n-1]$ right, $(n+1)/2$ elements, one more than $\min\{i,n-i\}$; Figure 2.3’s last step, $\mathrm{add}(4,z)$ with $n=9$, is such a case, and it shifts left as the prose says. The bound $O(1+\min\{i,n-i\})$ holds either way.

The code calls $\mathrm{front.add}(\mathrm{front.size}()-i,x)$. List position $i$ is $\mathit{front}$’s element $\mathrm{front.size}()-i-1$, and $x$, which comes before it in the list, goes after it in $\mathit{front}$’s reversed order, at $\mathrm{front.size}()-i$. With $\mathrm{front.size}()-i-1$, adding at position 1 of $a,b,c$ held in $\mathit{front}$ would give $a,b,x,c$. The cost (2.1) is $O(i+1)$ either way.
